title: Microeconomics
description: Microeconomics develops the ability to explain and improve decisions made by consumers, workers, firms, managers, and policymakers. Students use models, graphs, algebra, evidence, experiments, and cases to analyze scarcity, exchange, demand, production, costs, pricing, competition, strategy, labor, information, market failure, regulation, and welfare. The course culminates in an evidence-based recommendation that integrates mechanism, incentives, distribution, uncertainty, and implementation.

topics.title: Economic Reasoning, Scarcity, Choice, and Institutions
topics.description: Microeconomics begins with purposeful choice under constraints. This unit establishes the language of tradeoffs, incentives, marginal analysis, models, and institutions that students will use to interpret every later household, firm, and policy decision.

children.title: Scarcity and choice
children.description: Explain why limited time, income, talent, and productive resources force individuals and organizations to choose.

children.title: Wants, resources, constraints, and feasible sets
Tradeoffs in personal and organizational decisions
Efficiency, equity, and other decision criteria
Opportunity cost and marginal analysis
children.description: Evaluate a decision by comparing the best forgone alternative and the incremental benefits and costs of one more unit.

children.title: Marginal benefit, marginal cost, and stopping rules
Incentives, unintended consequences, and second-order effects
Models and economic reasoning
children.description: Use simplified representations to isolate a mechanism without confusing the model with the full complexity of reality.

children.title: Institutions, property rights, and exchange
children.description: Understand how rules, norms, contracts, and enforcement shape incentives and the gains available from exchange.

children.title: Voluntary exchange and gains from trade
Formal rules, informal norms, and enforcement
Power, bargaining position, and institutional context

topics.title: Specialization, Comparative Advantage, and Economic Evidence
topics.description: Good microeconomic analysis combines a theory of choice with disciplined use of evidence. Students connect production possibilities and comparative advantage to data literacy, experiments, and causal reasoning.

children.title: Production possibilities
children.description: Represent feasible combinations of outputs and use the frontier to explain scarcity, efficiency, and tradeoffs.

children.title: Points inside, on, and outside the frontier
Productive efficiency and unemployment of resources
Technology, resources, and shifts in capacity
Comparative advantage and specialization
children.description: Show why specialization can create gains even when one party is more productive in every activity.

children.title: Terms of trade and shared gains
Specialization limits, adjustment costs, and resilience
Describing economic evidence
children.description: Read tables, graphs, distributions, indexes, and summary statistics without overstating what the data show.

children.title: Levels, rates, shares, percentage changes, and elasticities
Visual scale, denominator, and aggregation choices
Causality and economic experiments
children.description: Distinguish association from causal effect and use counterfactual reasoning to evaluate claims.

children.title: External validity, heterogeneity, and ethical constraints

topics.title: Supply, Demand, and Market Equilibrium
topics.description: Supply and demand form the central coordination model of introductory microeconomics. Students learn to build the curves from behavior, locate equilibrium, and predict how a market responds to changing conditions.

children.title: Demand
children.description: Connect willingness to pay and consumer choice to the relationship between price and quantity demanded.

children.title: Movement along versus shift of demand
Income, tastes, expectations, population, and related goods
Reservation prices and the extensive versus intensive margin
Supply
children.description: Connect marginal cost and seller participation to the relationship between price and quantity supplied.

children.title: Movement along versus shift of supply
Input prices, technology, expectations, entry, and regulation
Reservation prices, shutdown, and capacity constraints
Equilibrium and adjustment
children.description: Explain how price coordinates plans and how shortages or surpluses create pressure for adjustment.

children.title: Stable versus unstable or constrained adjustment
Comparative statics
children.description: Predict the direction and relative size of market changes while holding other factors constant.

topics.title: Elasticity, Revenue, Incidence, and Market Intervention
topics.description: Elasticity turns the direction of a market response into a measure of magnitude. It is indispensable for pricing, forecasting, tax incidence, labor decisions, capacity planning, and policy evaluation.

children.title: Price elasticity of demand
children.description: Measure how strongly quantity demanded responds to price and interpret the result using economic context.

children.title: Substitutes, budget share, necessity, and time horizon
Revenue and pricing
children.description: Use elasticity to predict how price changes affect revenue while recognizing that revenue is not profit.

children.title: Capacity, variable cost, and contribution margin
Other elasticities
children.description: Use related responsiveness measures to forecast market interactions and business exposure.

children.title: Income elasticity and normal or inferior goods
Taxes, controls, and incidence
children.description: Analyze who truly bears a tax or regulation and how intervention changes quantity, surplus, and allocation.

children.title: Price ceilings, shortages, quality, and nonprice rationing
Price floors, surpluses, and minimum-wage framing

topics.title: Consumer Preferences, Utility, Choice, and Demand
topics.description: Consumer theory explains how people translate preferences and purchasing power into choices. The framework supports demand analysis, segmentation, financial decisions, benefits design, and evaluation of consumer welfare.

children.title: Preferences and utility
children.description: Represent rankings of alternatives while separating the usefulness of utility from claims about measurable happiness.

children.title: Indifference curves and marginal rate of substitution
Budget constraints
children.description: Describe the choice set created by income, prices, taxes, subsidies, borrowing limits, and nonprice constraints.

children.title: Quantity discounts, vouchers, and in-kind benefits
Time, attention, credit, and institutional constraints
Utility maximization
children.description: Locate the best affordable bundle and explain interior and corner solutions.

children.title: Demand and welfare
children.description: Derive demand responses from constrained choice and measure the value consumers receive from market access.

children.title: Consumer surplus, compensating variation intuition, and willingness to pay

topics.title: Behavioral Economics, Risk, and Intertemporal Choice
topics.description: Standard choice models are useful benchmarks, but real decisions involve uncertainty, time, limited attention, social preferences, and predictable biases. Students learn when the benchmark works and how to improve decision environments when it does not.

children.title: Choice under uncertainty
children.description: Compare risky alternatives using probabilities, payoffs, and attitudes toward risk.

children.title: Intertemporal choice
children.description: Analyze tradeoffs between present and future consumption, effort, investment, and wellbeing.

children.title: Judgment and decision biases
children.description: Recognize systematic deviations that affect pricing, saving, hiring, evaluation, and consumer behavior.

children.title: Overconfidence, projection bias, and limited attention
Defaults, salience, mental accounting, and choice architecture
Social preferences and fairness
children.description: Extend self-interest models to reciprocity, identity, norms, and perceived fairness.

children.title: Ethical design, manipulation risk, and welfare ambiguity

topics.title: Production, Productivity, and Cost
topics.description: Producer theory connects technology and input choices to cost, supply, scale, and operational performance. Students learn to distinguish accounting measures from the economic costs relevant to decisions.

children.title: Technology and production
children.description: Describe how labor, capital, materials, management, and technology become output.

children.title: Production functions and feasible input-output combinations
Input choice and productivity
children.description: Choose input combinations and diagnose productivity without mistaking correlation for causation.

children.title: Isoquant and marginal rate of technical substitution intuition
Total factor productivity and measurement challenges
Economic cost
children.description: Include opportunity costs and classify costs by how they change with the decision horizon and output.

children.title: Explicit, implicit, sunk, and opportunity costs
Fixed, variable, avoidable, and incremental costs
Scale, scope, and learning
children.description: Evaluate how size, product breadth, utilization, and accumulated experience change unit economics.

children.title: Returns to scale versus diminishing returns
Economies of scope and shared assets
Learning curves, capacity, bottlenecks, and network production

topics.title: Competitive Markets, Entry, Exit, and Welfare
topics.description: Perfect competition is both a model of price-taking behavior and a benchmark for evaluating other market structures. Students link firm decisions to market supply, entry, exit, and total surplus.

children.title: Price-taking firm
children.description: Explain why a competitive firm treats market price as given and chooses output where incremental benefit equals incremental cost.

children.title: Market price, firm demand, and marginal revenue
Profit maximization using marginal revenue and marginal cost
Market supply and equilibrium
children.description: Aggregate firm behavior and connect cost conditions to short-run market outcomes.

children.title: Entry, exit, and long-run adjustment
children.description: Show how economic profit attracts entry and losses induce exit, changing market supply over time.

children.title: Economic profit as an entry signal
Barriers to entry, mobility, and contestability
Welfare benchmark
children.description: Measure gains from trade and identify the assumptions behind competitive efficiency.

children.title: Distribution, missing markets, power, and other benchmark limits

topics.title: Monopoly, Market Power, and Strategic Pricing
topics.description: Firms with market power choose price or quantity while anticipating customer response. This unit develops profit-maximizing pricing, welfare analysis, price discrimination, and revenue-management applications.

children.title: Sources and measurement of market power
children.description: Identify why competition may be limited and evaluate market boundaries carefully.

children.title: Barriers from scale, control, regulation, switching, and data
Concentration ratios, HHI, markup, and Lerner-index intuition
Single-price monopoly
children.description: Derive the monopolist's output and price choice and compare it with the competitive benchmark.

children.title: Profit, consumer surplus, and deadweight loss
Price discrimination
children.description: Explain when charging different effective prices can raise profit, expand output, or redistribute surplus.

children.title: First-, second-, and third-degree price discrimination
Versioning, bundling, coupons, and nonlinear tariffs
Equity, privacy, fairness, and legal considerations
Revenue management
children.description: Apply demand, elasticity, capacity, and timing to perishable inventory and constrained service businesses.

children.title: Hospitality, travel, entertainment, and subscription applications

topics.title: Oligopoly, Game Theory, and Strategic Interaction
topics.description: When a few firms or decision makers affect one another, the best action depends on anticipated responses. Game theory supplies a disciplined way to reason about competition, coordination, bargaining, and credible commitments.

children.title: Elements of a game
children.description: Represent a strategic situation through players, actions, information, timing, payoffs, and rules.

children.title: Players, strategies, actions, outcomes, and payoffs
Dominance and Nash equilibrium
children.description: Predict mutually consistent choices while recognizing that equilibrium need not be efficient or unique.

children.title: Coordination failure, multiple equilibria, and mixed-strategy awareness
Oligopoly models
children.description: Compare how assumptions about strategic variables and timing change prices, quantities, profits, and welfare.

children.title: Dynamic strategy and cooperation
children.description: Assess commitment, credibility, reputation, bargaining, and the sustainability of cooperation.

children.title: Backward induction and subgame perfection intuition
Repeated games, punishment, and tacit coordination
Bargaining power, outside options, and negotiation

topics.title: Product Differentiation, Auctions, Platforms, and Digital Markets
topics.description: Modern competition often turns on differentiated products, allocation mechanisms, data, and network effects rather than a single posted price. Students analyze these settings without abandoning the core logic of demand, cost, and strategy.

children.title: Product differentiation
children.description: Explain how location, quality, brand, service, and switching costs soften price competition.

children.title: Variety, fixed costs, and monopolistic competition
Auctions and procurement
children.description: Understand how auction rules aggregate information and shape bidding incentives.

children.title: English, Dutch, first-price, and second-price formats
Winner's curse and bid shading intuition
Reserve prices, procurement, and collusion risk
Network effects and standards
children.description: Analyze products whose value depends on adoption by other users or complementary products.

children.title: Critical mass, tipping, and path dependence
Platforms and two-sided markets
children.description: Set prices and participation rules when a platform must attract multiple interdependent user groups.

children.title: Platform governance, ranking, access, and take rates
Data advantage, self-preferencing, and competition policy

topics.title: Factor Markets, Labor Economics, and Human Capital
topics.description: Labor and other input markets determine wages, employment, rents, and the distribution of income. This unit applies marginal analysis to hiring, compensation, human-capital investment, mobility, bargaining, and discrimination.

children.title: Derived demand for inputs
children.description: Connect demand for labor and capital to the value of the output those inputs help produce.

children.title: Marginal product and marginal revenue product
Value of marginal product under competition
Input demand shifts from technology, prices, and product demand
Labor supply and job choice
children.description: Analyze how wages, benefits, schedules, risk, and nonmonetary conditions affect participation and hours.

children.title: Human capital and compensation
children.description: Evaluate education, training, experience, and incentive pay as investments and organizational choices.

children.title: Tournaments, bonuses, commissions, and team incentives
Benefits, deferred compensation, retention, and sorting
Labor-market institutions and inequality
children.description: Examine how bargaining, monopsony, discrimination, mobility, and policy affect wages and employment.

children.title: Minimum wages, unions, and collective bargaining
Occupational segregation, pay gaps, mobility, and measurement

topics.title: Information Economics, Incentives, Contracts, and Organizations
topics.description: Transactions can fail when parties possess different information or take actions that others cannot observe. Students use screening, signaling, monitoring, and contract design to improve markets and organizations.

children.title: Asymmetric information
children.description: Identify who knows what, when they know it, and how hidden information changes trade.

children.title: Adverse selection and screening
children.description: Design choices that sort participants when hidden types affect expected cost or value.

children.title: Hiring, lending, insurance, and customer applications
Moral hazard and principal-agent problems
children.description: Align incentives when effort, care, or risk-taking cannot be perfectly observed after an agreement.

children.title: Sales, executive, lending, and team applications
Contracts and organizational boundaries
children.description: Choose governance and contract terms that allocate rights, risks, control, and surplus.

children.title: Make-or-buy, outsourcing, franchising, and vertical integration
Authority, delegation, culture, and relational contracts

topics.title: Externalities, Public Goods, Common Resources, and Sustainability
topics.description: Private choices may impose costs or benefits not reflected in market prices, and some valuable goods are difficult to finance through ordinary exchange. Students diagnose the failure before selecting a remedy.

children.title: Externalities
children.description: Compare private and social incentives when one party's action affects others outside a transaction.

children.title: Marginal private and social benefits or costs
Policy and bargaining responses
children.description: Match a remedy to the mechanism, information, enforcement capacity, and distributional context.

children.title: Coasean bargaining, property rights, and transaction costs
Public goods and common resources
children.description: Classify goods by rivalry and excludability and explain free riding or overuse.

children.title: Private, club, common-pool, and public goods
Tragedy of the commons and congestion
Community governance, pricing, quotas, and public provision
Sustainability and climate economics
children.description: Use microeconomic tools to analyze environmental risk, carbon, adaptation, innovation, and intergenerational tradeoffs.

children.title: Abatement cost and policy instrument choice
Discounting, uncertainty, resilience, and just transition

topics.title: Welfare, Equity, Regulation, Antitrust, and Market Design
topics.description: The capstone unit asks when markets work, when they fail, how gains and losses are distributed, and whether an intervention improves outcomes in practice. Students integrate theory, evidence, implementation, and uncertainty into an actionable recommendation.

children.title: Welfare and distribution
children.description: Evaluate total gains while making distributional choices and ethical assumptions explicit.

children.title: Incidence across income, region, identity, and time
Social welfare functions and limits of aggregation
Regulation and antitrust
children.description: Assess market power, conduct, remedies, and regulatory tradeoffs using evidence rather than concentration alone.

children.title: Market definition, concentration, entry, and competitive effects
Cartels, exclusion, tying, vertical restraints, and mergers
Innovation, dynamic competition, error costs, and remedy design
Market design
children.description: Treat market rules as design variables that influence participation, information, matching, and outcomes.

children.title: Matching markets and allocation without prices
School choice, kidney exchange, and labor matching examples
Incentive compatibility, robustness, fairness, and gaming
Integrated microeconomic decision
children.description: Build and defend a recommendation that combines a behavioral model, evidence, stakeholder effects, and implementation plan.

children.title: Decision question, alternatives, baseline, and mechanism
Winners, losers, unintended consequences, and ethics
Recommendation, implementation, metrics, and post-decision review
